├── generation/
│   ├── prompt.py            # Prompt construction
│   └── answer.py            # LLM call + citations
├── api/
│   └── server.py            # FastAPI app
└── ask/
    └── index.html           # GitHub Pages frontend

id: building RAG for my website_Core Goals_0
text: -**Ask questions** about my blogs, ideas, and explanations. -**Get short, grounded answers** exclusively from my own writing. -**Context-aware retrieval:** Fetch code when I ask for implementation, or explanations when I ask “why”.

id: building RAG for my website_Core Goals_1
text: -**Zero Hallucinations:** Never invent facts beyond the source material. -**Local Execution:** Run entirely locally (no paid APIs required).

id: building RAG for my website_Phase 1: Ingestion & Corpus Creation_0
text: **Goal:** Turn messy, real-world blog content into clean, inspectable retrieval units.

id: building RAG for my website_1. Loading Blog Data_0
text: All my blog posts already exist as Markdown files in my GitHub repository. `load_github.py` simply fetches them directly from the source. This part was straightforward.

id: building RAG for my website_2. Parsing Markdown (Harder Than Expected)_0
text: Markdown can be messy. `parse_markdown.py` extracts structured data: * **Frontmatter:** Title, date, categories. * **Structure:** Section headings, paragraphs, code blocks, and links.

id: building RAG for my website_2. Parsing Markdown (Harder Than Expected)_1
text: I avoided using a heavy-weight Markdown AST parser and instead relied on careful regex and structure matching. This gave me more control but was trickier to get right than I initially expected.

id: building RAG for my website_3. Cleaning Without Summarizing_0
text: The script `clean_text.py` handles normalization: * Normalizes whitespace. * Removes non-content "junk". * **Crucially:** Does *not* rewrite or summarize. * Preserves the original author's voice.

id: building RAG for my website_3. Cleaning Without Summarizing_1
text: This is vital because **RAG quality starts with data integrity**. If the source data is lost or mutated, the retrieval will be flawed.

id: building RAG for my website_4. Chunking (The Most Important Step)_0
text: I spent the majority of my time on `chunker.py`. A **chunk** is the smallest piece of text that should be retrieved on its own to answer a question.

id: building RAG for my website_4. Chunking (The Most Important Step)_1
text: **My Chunking Rules:** * One paragraph = one chunk. * Multiple sentences are fine. * Multiple distinct ideas are *not* fine in one chunk. * **Code blocks** are treated as separate chunks. * **Links** are embedded in text, not standalone. * Chunks must be **self-contained**. * Max length: ~200–300 words.

id: building RAG for my website_4. Chunking (The Most Important Step)_2
text: **Example Output:**

id: building RAG for my website_4. Chunking (The Most Important Step)_3
building RAG for my website_Embeddings_0
text: I utilize the **Sentence Transformers** library for generating embeddings:

id: building RAG for my website_Embeddings_1
text: SentenceTransformerEmbeddings("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

id: building RAG for my website_Embeddings_2
text: * **384-dimensional vectors** * Fast inference * Runs locally * Excellent performance for semantic search

id: building RAG for my website_Embeddings_3
text: Both text and code are embedded using the same model, but they are flagged via metadata to distinguish between them during retrieval.

id: building RAG for my website_Vector Store (FAISS)_0
text: I use **FAISS** (Facebook AI Similarity Search) to store the vectors efficiently. Since FAISS only stores the vectors themselves, I maintain a parallel metadata store:

id: building RAG for my website_Vector Store (FAISS)_1
text:
vector → embedding
payload → { id, text, metadata }

id: building RAG for my website_Vector Store (FAISS)_2
text: **Query Example:** * **Query:** “Why do we use softmax in MNIST?” * **Returns:** * **Distance:** 0.29 * **Chunk:** "Softmax is used in MNIST classification..."

id: building RAG for my website_Phase 3: Retrieval Control & Reranking_0
text: Raw semantic search isn’t always enough. User intent varies.

id: building RAG for my website_Phase 3: Retrieval Control & Reranking_1
text: * If I ask **“show me code”** → I want code blocks. * If I ask **“why does this work”** → I want conceptual explanations.

id: building RAG for my website_Phase 3: Retrieval Control & Reranking_2
text: To handle this, `retrieve.py` implements an intent-aware pipeline:

id: building RAG for my website_Phase 3: Retrieval Control & Reranking_3
text:
query
  ↓
intent classification
  ↓
embedding
  ↓
FAISS search
  ↓
intent-aware reranking
  ↓
top-k chunks

id: building RAG for my website_Phase 3: Retrieval Control & Reranking_4
text: This step alone improved answer quality dramatically by filtering out irrelevant chunk types (e.g., ignoring text chunks when the user explicitly wants code).

id: building RAG for my website_Prompt Construction_0
text: Context is king. I explicitly tell the LLM what each retrieved chunk represents to avoid confusion:

id: building RAG for my website_Prompt Construction_1
text:
[TEXT]
explanation...

[CODE]
code snippet...

id: building RAG for my website_Prompt Construction_2
text: Then I append the user's question. This simple formatting prevents the model from "guessing" the context type.

id: building RAG for my website_Generation (Local LLM)_0
text: I rely on **Ollama** for local inference:

id: building RAG for my website_Generation (Local LLM)_1
text:
ollama serve
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b

id: building RAG for my website_Generation (Local LLM)_2
text: * **No cloud APIs** * **No token limits** * **No costs**

id: building RAG for my website_Citations & Grounding_0
text: The system is designed to never hallucinate sources. Instead, it: 1. Tracks exactly which chunks were used to generate the answer. 2. Returns specific citations alongside the answer.

id: building RAG for my website_Citations & Grounding_1
text: **Example Response:** > **Answer:** Softmax converts logits into probabilities... > > **Sources:** > * `600+ leetcode questions: lessons_intro_0` (text, section=intro)

id: building RAG for my website_Persistence_0
text: The FAISS index and metadata are persisted to disk. On restart: * No re-embedding required. * No re-indexing required. * **Instant retrieval.**

id: building RAG for my website_Persistence_1
text: This persistence is what separates a toy script from a usable tool.

id: building RAG for my website_Frontend & Deployment_0
text: * **UI:** Lives at [samitmohan.github.io/ask](/ask) * **Backend:** FastAPI * **Connectivity:** Cloudflare Tunnel (to expose the local server securely) * **Rendering:** Markdown + Sources

id: building RAG for my website_Frontend & Deployment_1
text: **Final Pipeline:**

id: building RAG for my website_Frontend & Deployment_2
text: 1. **GitHub Pages UI** captures input. 2. **FastAPI backend** processes the request. 3. **FAISS** performs retrieval. 4. **Reranker** optimizes results based on intent. 5. **Local LLM** generates the response. 6. **UI** renders the grounded answer + sources.

id: building RAG for my website_Final Thoughts_0
text: This project taught me several key lessons about building AI systems:

id: building RAG for my website_Final Thoughts_1
text: 1. **RAG is mostly data engineering**, not just model selection. 2. **Chunking strategy** matters more than the specific embedding model. 3. **Intent control** beats simply using larger embeddings. 4. **Local LLMs** are surprisingly capable for many real-world use cases.

id: building RAG for my website_Final Thoughts_2
text: And most importantly:

id: building RAG for my website_Final Thoughts_3
text: > **Building something for yourself teaches you far more than building a demo.**
